weeks.title: Hello, little one
weeks.head: These first days are all about feeding, sleeping and getting to know each other.
t: {She} sees light, shapes and faces, and sees best about 20–30 cm away. That’s about the distance to your face during a feed.
Hunger signs: hands to mouth, turning towards the breast or bottle, smacking lips. Breast milk or formula is all {she} needs for now.
Expect lots of sleep in short stretches, day and night: 14–17 hours in every 24 for the first 3 months.
Every sleep: on {pos} back, on a firm flat surface, in {pos} own crib in your room, with nothing soft in it.
play: Hold {her} close and talk softly. By one month {she} will know your voice.
Cuddle and hold {her} often. You can’t spoil a baby by holding or responding to them.
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.

weeks.title: Crying is talking
weeks.head: Crying is how {she} tells you something: hungry, tired, too hot, or wanting a cuddle.
t: {Pos} eyes may sometimes wander or cross. That’s normal while {she} learns to use both eyes together.
You may notice a little milk coming back up during or after feeds. It’s very common and nothing to worry about while {she's} happy and gaining weight.
Fussing and crying can add up to about 2 hours a day in these early weeks. That’s normal, and it eases after 8–9 weeks.
Ask your doctor about vitamin D drops: 400 IU a day from soon after birth, breastfed babies included.
play: Try holding, gentle rocking, a walk in the carrier, or soft background noise.
If you need a break, put {her} down safely on {pos} back and step away for a few minutes. That’s okay.
watch: A weak or high-pitched cry, or a cry that doesn’t sound like {pos} usual cry, needs urgent help.

weeks.title: Talk, read, sing
weeks.head: Talking, reading and singing from day one helps {her} understand language later.
t: You may notice {her} watching your face closely during feeds and cuddles.
{She} loves your voice most of all, especially when it’s a little higher, slower and sing-song.
Signs {she's} full: closing {pos} mouth or turning {pos} head away. If {she} isn’t hungry, it’s fine to stop.
Some days feel fussier than others, and evenings are often the hardest, usually between 6 pm and midnight.
play: Read anything out loud, even your own book.
Sing to {her}, any song you know.

weeks.title: Tummy time begins
weeks.head: Short spells of tummy time while {she's} awake build neck and shoulder strength.
t: By one month, {she} can pick out your voice, even from another room.
Around now, {she} will focus on your face when you cradle {her}.
You may see short head lifts while {she's} on {pos} tummy, and arms and legs moving a lot.
Tummy time is only for awake, watched play. Sleep is always on {pos} back.
play: Lay {her} tummy-down on a play mat for a minute or two, a few times a day, while you watch. Build up to 30 minutes a day in total.
During tummy time, put a toy at eye level in front of {her} to encourage lifting {pos} head.
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.

weeks.title: Looking at you
weeks.head: Faces are {pos} favourite thing to look at, and yours is the best of all.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} look at your face and calm down when you talk to {her} or pick {her} up, by 2 months.
You may notice {her} watching you as you move around the room.
{She} may follow your face a little way, then lose it as it crosses from one side to the other. That’s expected until about 2 months.
Keep {her} in the same room as you for every sleep, day and night, for at least the first 6 months.
play: Get close, face to face, and make slow, big expressions.
Watch {pos} signals: eye contact and sounds mean “play with me”; turning away, yawning or fussing mean “I need a break”.

weeks.title: Hello, smiles
weeks.head: It’s highly likely you’ll see {pos} first real smiles around now.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} smile back when you talk or smile at {her}, by 2 months. {She} may seem happy to see you when you walk up.
{She} sees you best about 20–30 cm away. If {pos} eyes wander now and then, that’s normal and usually settles by 2–3 months.
You may notice a little milk coming back up after feeds. It usually settles by {pos} first birthday as the muscle at the top of {pos} tummy gets stronger.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} hold {pos} head up during tummy time, by 2 months.
Evenings may be fussier for now. Crying runs at about 2 hours a day in the first 6 weeks and eases after 8–9 weeks.
play: Smile and talk, then pause. Give {her} time to answer with a look or a sound.
Put your phone away during play, so you notice and answer {pos} signals.

weeks.title: First sounds
weeks.head: Soft sounds other than crying start to appear.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear sounds other than crying, and see {her} react to loud sounds, by 2 months.
Coughing, hiccups or gulping during feeds can be part of reflux. Holding {her} upright during and after feeds, and burping during feeds, can help.
Help {her} learn night from day: lights low and voices quiet at night; curtains open and play in the day.
play: Copy {pos} sounds back, like a little conversation.
Talk and play during feeding, dressing and bath time.
watch: Same day if {she} vomits green or yellow, vomits very forcefully, or there is blood in {pos} vomit or poop.

weeks.title: Strong neck
weeks.head: Head control is building fast.
t: Around 2 months, {she} will start following your face from one side to the other and back again.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} hold {pos} head up on {pos} tummy, move both arms and legs, and open {pos} hands briefly, by 2 months.
Keep naps safe too: on {pos} back, on a firm flat surface.
play: Hold a rattle to one side of {pos} head, shake it, and see if {she} looks for the sound.
Keep up tummy time, a little more each day.
watch: Under 3 months, a temperature of 38 °C or higher needs urgent medical advice.

weeks.title: 2-month check-up
weeks.head: A nice week to jot down questions for {pos} 2-month check-up.
t: You may hear {her} coo, repeating vowel sounds like “ah-ah-ah” and “ooh-ooh-ooh”.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} look at a toy for several seconds and watch you as you move, by 2 months.
play: When {she's} upset, stay calm: talk softly, hold, rock or sing.
Look after yourself too. It’s easier to enjoy {her} when you feel okay.
watch: You know {her} best. If something worries you, or {she} stops doing something {she} could do before, bring it up with your doctor.

weeks.title: Calmer days ahead
weeks.head: Fussing and crying tend to ease from around now.
t: You may see {her} look at you, move or make sounds to get your attention.
If {she} cries a lot but is otherwise well, colic usually stops by 3–4 months. Holding {her} upright during feeds and burping afterwards can help.
Crying tends to drop after 8–9 weeks, to about 1 hour a day by 10–12 weeks.
play: Short walks outside: point at things and name them.
Notice what {she} reacts to, so you learn what {she} likes and doesn’t like.

weeks.title: Cooing conversations
weeks.head: Coos like “oooo” and “aahh” are coming.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear {her} coo and make sounds back when you talk, by 4 months.
{She's} learning to focus on faces and close objects.
Steady routines for sleep and feeds can help the days feel calmer.
play: Talk, wait, and answer each coo. This back-and-forth builds language.
Use {pos} name often so {she} learns it.

weeks.title: Following with the eyes
weeks.head: Moving things are fascinating right now.
t: By 3 months, {she} will follow a moving object with {pos} eyes, and focus on faces and close objects.
Crying has usually settled to around an hour a day by now.
No screen time is recommended at this age. Talking and reading are better for {her}.
play: Lay {her} on {pos} back and move a bright toy slowly from side to side, and up and down.
Lay {her} on a blanket with safe toys to reach for and kick at.

weeks.title: Smiling to get your attention
weeks.head: {She's} starting conversations now, not just answering.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} smile on {pos} own to get your attention, and chuckle when you play, by 4 months.
You may notice {her} looking at {pos} hands with interest.
Naps count too: always on {pos} back, flat and firm.
play: Play simple face games and see what makes {her} chuckle.
Play peek-a-boo: cover your eyes, uncover them and say “peek-a-boo!”

weeks.title: Reaching out
weeks.head: Hands are getting busy.
t: {Pos} colour vision is getting better, and round shapes like faces, spirals and bull’s-eyes are extra interesting.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} hold a toy you put in {pos} hand and swing at toys, by 4 months.
Try not to keep {her} in a swing, bouncer or stroller for more than 1 hour at a time.
play: Hang or hold a toy within reach so {she} can bat at it.
Give easy-to-hold toys, like a rattle or a cloth book.

weeks.title: Hands to mouth
weeks.head: Exploring with the mouth is how {she} learns.
t: {She's} more tuned in to your tone of voice now. An upbeat voice may get a smile or a coo.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} bring {pos} hands to {pos} mouth, by 4 months.
Offer safe things to mouth: nothing sharp, hot, or small enough to choke on.
play: Sing while you gently move {pos} arms and legs, a little baby workout.
Copy {pos} sounds and see how long you can keep the back-and-forth going.

weeks.title: Mini push-ups
weeks.head: Tummy time is turning into mini push-ups.
t: You may hear lots of babbling, like “muh-muh” and “bah-bah”.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} push up onto {pos} elbows on {pos} tummy, and hold {pos} head steady when you hold {her}, by 4 months.
From 4 months, 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included, is a healthy amount.
play: Get down on the floor at eye level during tummy time.
Hold {her} under the arms with {pos} feet on your lap and let {her} bounce.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.

weeks.title: 4-month check-up
weeks.head: A nice week to note questions for {pos} 4-month check-up.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} open {pos} mouth at the breast or bottle when hungry, by 4 months.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} turn {pos} head towards your voice, by 4 months.
4-month vaccines (Singapore): DTaP-IPV-Hib dose 2 and pneumococcal (PCV) dose 1.
play: Make time for floor play several times a day.
Share a picture book: point at the pictures and name them.
watch: You know {her} best. If something worries you, or {she} stops doing something {she} could do before, bring it up with your doctor.
If colic-like crying carries on after 4 months, mention it to your doctor.

weeks.title: Laughing together
weeks.head: Real laughs are on the way.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear {her} laugh, and see {her} know familiar people, by 6 months.
Breast milk or formula is still all {she} needs. Chewing fists, waking more at night or wanting extra feeds don’t mean {she's} ready for solids.
play: Find the games that make {her} laugh, and repeat them.
Back-and-forth play: when {she} smiles, smile back; when {she} makes sounds, copy them.

weeks.title: Teething may start
weeks.head: First teeth can come any time in the first year, often around 6 months.
t: Signs of teething: sore red gums, more dribbling, chewing on things, one flushed cheek, rubbing an ear, fussier sleep.
Teething can raise {pos} temperature slightly, but not to 38 °C. There’s no evidence it causes diarrhoea.
play: Note teething signs in Goldfox so you can spot a pattern.
Share a book every day: reading together builds language and closeness.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.

weeks.title: Raspberries and squeals
weeks.head: {She's} playing with sounds.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear {her} take turns making sounds with you, blow raspberries and squeal, by 6 months.
Reading together every day supports language and closeness.
play: Blow raspberries back and take turns.
“Read” by talking about colourful pictures, and answer {pos} babble: “Yes, that’s the doggy!”

weeks.title: Grab and explore
weeks.head: Reaching is getting accurate.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} reach for a toy {she} wants, and put things in {pos} mouth to explore, by 6 months.
{Pos} eye colour may still be changing. It can keep shifting until about {pos} first birthday.
Check toys aren’t small enough to choke on.
play: Put toys just out of reach to encourage rolling and reaching.
When {she} looks at something, point to it and talk about it.

weeks.title: Rolling over
weeks.head: Rolling opens up a new way to move.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} roll from tummy to back, by 6 months. Sitting without support can come any time from about 4 to 9 months.
play: Give lots of floor play, several times a day.
Hold {her} sitting up with toys to look at while {she} learns to balance.
watch: From 3 to 6 months, get urgent advice for 39 °C or higher, or a high temperature with other signs of illness.

weeks.title: Mirror, mirror
weeks.head: {She's} getting curious about faces, including {pos} own.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} enjoy looking in a mirror, by 6 months.
By 6 months, {she} can tell objects apart by how they look.
Standing with your help can start any time from about 5 to 11 months.
play: Sit together in front of a mirror and name body parts.
Try whispers, claps and funny noises, and see which ones {she} likes.

weeks.title: Getting ready for food
weeks.head: First foods come at around 6 months, not before.
t: Signs {she's} ready for food: sitting up with a steady head, picking food up and bringing it to {pos} mouth, and swallowing food rather than spitting it out.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} push up on straight arms on {pos} tummy, and lean on {pos} hands when sitting, by 6 months.
Ask your doctor about starting solids, especially if {she} was born early.
play: Let {her} sit with you at family meals to see how eating works.
Hold {her} under the arms to stand, look around together and name what you see.

weeks.title: Hungry or full?
weeks.head: Learning {pos} food signals makes mealtimes easier.
t: Hungry: opening {pos} mouth for the spoon, getting excited about food. Full: pushing food away, closing {pos} mouth, turning away.
Peanut foods given in infancy can help prevent peanut allergy. If {she} has eczema or a food allergy, ask your doctor first.
play: Follow {pos} lead. Getting used to eating matters more than how much.
When {she} drops a toy, pick it up and give it back. This game teaches cause and effect.

weeks.title: Half a year!
weeks.head: Six months: first foods, new vaccines and lots of new sounds.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} close {pos} lips to show {she} doesn’t want more food, by 6 months.
By now {pos} eyes should stay lined up together, even if one is briefly covered.
Start with small amounts alongside breast milk or formula.
6-month vaccines (Singapore): 6-in-1 dose 3 and PCV dose 2. A flu vaccine is recommended every year from 6 months to under 5 years.
play: Sing to {her} and play music.
Read {pos} mood: if {she's} happy, keep going; if {she's} upset, take a break and comfort {her}.
watch: You know {her} best. If something worries you, or {she} stops doing something {she} could do before, bring it up with your doctor.
From 6 months, if one eye doesn’t always look the same way as the other, tell {pos} doctor.

weeks.title: First tastes
weeks.head: Variety from the start helps later eating.
t: Breast milk or formula still gives {her} most of {pos} energy. Offer vegetables, including less sweet ones, not just carrot and sweet potato.
Front teeth are usually the first to come through, around 6 months.
No added salt or sugar, including stock cubes and gravy. Cows’ milk can go in food, but not as a main drink until 1 year.
play: Let {her} touch, hold and squish food. It’s all learning.
Keep mealtimes calm, with no TV, phone or tablet at the table.
watch: Reflux that starts for the first time after 6 months is worth a visit to your doctor.

weeks.title: Naming the world
weeks.head: {She's} starting to link words with things.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} look when you call {pos} name, by 9 months.
Egg, peanut, gluten and fish can be offered from around 6 months, one at a time, so you can spot any reaction.
play: On walks, point at cars, trees and animals and name them.
Repeat {pos} sounds and add a word: “bababa… book!”

weeks.title: Safe finger foods
weeks.head: Food safety matters as textures get bigger.
t: Gagging, with watery eyes, tongue pushed forward and retching, is part of learning to eat. If {she} prefers smooth food for now, keep offering lumpier textures and {she} will get used to them.
Avoid whole nuts and hard foods like raw carrot or apple. Cut small round foods like grapes into quarters.
play: Try soft finger foods {she} can pick up.
Stay close while {she} explores, so {she} knows you’re near.

weeks.title: Peekaboo!
weeks.head: Hiding and finding games are a hit.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} smile or laugh when you play peekaboo, by 9 months.
{She's} learning that things still exist when they’re out of sight.
Standing alone can come any time from about 7 to 17 months.
play: Play peekaboo with a cloth over your head and see if {she} pulls it off.
Hide behind a door and leave a foot in view as a clue.

weeks.title: Mama-ma, ba-ba-ba
weeks.head: Babbling chains are coming.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear lots of different sounds like “mamamama” and “babababa”, by 9 months.
The teeth either side of the front ones usually follow, around 8 months.
play: Babble back and add the real word: “ba-ba… yes, ball!”
Keep reading every day and let {her} touch the pages.

weeks.title: Bang, bang!
weeks.head: Making noise is how {she} experiments.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} bang two things together, by 9 months. Two or three minutes with one toy is plenty right now.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} pass things from one hand to the other, by 9 months.
Keep anything small enough to choke on out of reach.
play: Dump blocks out of a container and put them back in together.
Give pots, pans or a small drum and let {her} make noise.

weeks.title: A little shy
weeks.head: Shyness with new people is a sign of {pos} bond with you.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} get shy or clingy around strangers, and react when you leave, by 9 months. It shows how much {she} trusts you.
play: Let {her} warm up to new people from your lap.
Say a quick, cheerful goodbye instead of sneaking away, and say hello when you’re back.

weeks.title: Where did it go?
weeks.head: {She} knows things still exist when they’re out of sight.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} look for things dropped out of sight, like a spoon or a toy, by 9 months.
Screen time still isn’t recommended under 1 year. Reading and storytelling are better.
play: Hide a toy under a cloth while {she} watches, then let {her} find it.
Play “my turn, your turn” by passing a toy back and forth.

weeks.title: On the move
weeks.head: Crawling can start any time from about 5 to 13½ months, and skipping it is fine too.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} sit without support, by 9 months. If {she} goes straight from sitting to standing without crawling, that’s fine.
Clear a safe floor space, and move sharp or breakable things out of reach.
play: Put toys a little out of reach and cheer when {she} gets there by crawling, scooting or rolling.
Teach waving bye-bye and simple baby signs, so {she} can tell you what {she} wants.

weeks.title: Little self-feeder
weeks.head: Messy eating is learning.
t: Let {her} practise finger foods and sips from an open cup. Expect spills.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} “rake” food towards {her} with {pos} fingers, by 9 months. Walking alone can come any time from about 8 to 18 months, so there’s no rush.
play: Sit and eat together. {She} learns by watching you.
Point to pictures in books and name them.

weeks.title: Pick me up!
weeks.head: {She} can ask with gestures now.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see several expressions, like happy, sad, angry and surprised, by 9 months.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} lift {pos} arms to be picked up, by 9 months.
Keep offering new tastes and textures. It can take many tries before a food is liked.
play: Name feelings as you see them: “You look surprised!”
When {she} reaches or points, answer with words: “Up? Here we go!”

weeks.title: Sitting up solo
weeks.head: New positions, new views.
t: {She} loves dropping, rolling and throwing things to see what happens. It’s how {she} learns how the world works.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} get into a sitting position on {pos} own, by 9 months.
play: Say what you’d like {her} to do: “time to sit” rather than “don’t stand”.
Everyday things make great toys: wooden spoons, egg boxes, plastic tubs.

weeks.title: 9-month check-up
weeks.head: A nice week to note questions for {pos} 9-month check-up. A general development check is recommended around now.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} react when you leave the room, by looking, reaching for you or crying, by 9 months.
Ask about the 9-month developmental screening at {pos} visit.
play: Keep up daily floor play, reading and songs.
Stay close while {she} explores, so {she} knows you’re near.
watch: You know {her} best. If something worries you, or {she} stops doing something {she} could do before, bring it up with your doctor.

weeks.title: Bye-bye!
weeks.head: Gestures are words before words.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} wave bye-bye, by 12 months.
{She} will keep searching for a hidden toy, sure it’s still there somewhere.
Keep offering foods {she} turned down before. Tastes change.
play: Wave hello and bye-bye to people, pets and even the bathwater.
Talk or sing about what you’re doing: “This is the way we wash our hands.”

weeks.title: Understanding “no”
weeks.head: {She} understands more than {she} can say.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} understand “no”, pausing or stopping when you say it, by 12 months.
Try not to keep {her} strapped in (stroller, high chair, carrier) for more than 1 hour at a time.
play: Use short, clear words, and show what to do instead.
Show the behaviour you want and praise it with words and hugs.

weeks.title: Pulling up
weeks.head: Furniture becomes a climbing frame.
t: {Pos} attention span is growing. By 12 months {she} may stay with one toy for up to 15 minutes.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} pull up to stand, by 12 months.
Check that what {she} pulls up on is stable.
play: Place toys along the sofa to encourage cruising.
Play together with blocks and other toys that get little hands working.

weeks.title: Cruising
weeks.head: First steps, holding on.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} walk holding on to furniture, by 12 months. Walking with your help can start any time from about 6 to 14 months.
Being active several times a day is good for {her}; more is better.
play: Point out interesting things you see, like a bus, a bird or a dog.
Share books with flaps to lift or things to touch.

weeks.title: Pincer grasp
weeks.head: Tiny fingers, tiny bits.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} pick things up between thumb and pointer finger, like small bits of food, by 12 months.
Cut small round foods like grapes and cherry tomatoes into quarters.
play: Offer soft, small finger foods to practise.
Hand {her} a hairbrush, cup or spoon and watch {her} copy you.

weeks.title: Mama or dada
weeks.head: A special name for you is coming.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll hear {her} call you “mama”, “dada” or another special name, by 12 months.
{She} may start using things the way you do, like holding a toy phone to {pos} ear.
play: Build on what {she} says: if {she} says “ta”, say “Yes, a truck!”
Talk through everyday tasks. Every word counts.

weeks.title: In and out
weeks.head: Putting things in containers is a big thinking step.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} put something in a container, like a block in a cup, by 12 months.
Floor play several times a day is how {she} practises new skills.
play: Play “in and out” with blocks and a box.
With a new caregiver, give {her} time to get to know them, and bring a favourite toy or blanket.

weeks.title: Hide and seek
weeks.head: {She} remembers where things went.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} look for things {she} saw you hide, like a toy under a blanket, by 12 months.
The first back teeth (molars) usually come through around 12 months.
play: Hide a toy under one of two cups and let {her} find it.
Let {her} choose the bedtime book.

weeks.title: Baby-proofing, round two
weeks.head: A busier explorer needs a safer home.
t: {She} may empty drawers and bins to see what’s inside. That’s curiosity at work, so add safety locks where needed.
Move sharp or breakable things out of reach, and lock away medicines, chemicals and cleaning products. Save your local poison or emergency number in your phone.
play: Get down to {pos} height and look for hazards.
Show {her} how to stroke a soft toy or a pet gently, and praise {her} when {she} does.

weeks.title: Cup practice
weeks.head: Drinking skills are developing.
t: Drinks: water, breast milk or formula. No sugary drinks; juice isn’t needed.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} drink from an open cup while you hold it, by 12 months.
play: Offer water in an open cup with meals.
Let {her} hold a spoon of {pos} own at mealtimes.

weeks.title: Pat-a-cake
weeks.head: Games with rhythm and rules.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} play games with you, like pat-a-cake, by 12 months.
Screen time still isn’t recommended. Shared reading, songs and play are best.
play: Sing action songs and pause before the clap so {she} can join in.
Read together every day, and let {her} turn the pages.

weeks.title: Sleep before one
weeks.head: {Pos} sleep pattern is {pos} own. Up to 12 months, 12–16 hours a day, naps included, is a healthy amount.
t: From 1 to 2 years, 11–14 hours a day is a healthy amount.
play: Keep the bedtime routine the same each night: bath, book, song.
Bedtime routines are lovely one-to-one time together.

weeks.title: Happy first birthday!
weeks.head: One year! Look back at how far {she's} come.
t: It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} wave bye-bye and understand “no” by now.
{Pos} eye colour has mostly settled by now.
It’s highly likely you’ll see {her} pull up to stand and cruise along furniture by now. Walking alone can come any time up to about 18 months.
12-month vaccines (Singapore): MMR dose 1, chickenpox (varicella) dose 1 and the PCV booster. Cows’ milk can now be a main drink.
play: Celebrate with {pos} favourite song and a photo for Moments.
Look back at photos from week 1 together.
watch: You know {her} best. If something worries you, or {she} stops doing something {she} could do before, bring it up with your doctor.
